name: WebGL shader precision formats
plain: Reads float and integer precision ranges the GPU shader units support.
meaning: Mobile GPUs report different mediump and highp precision, so the numbers separate desktop, Apple, Adreno, Mali and PowerVR families.

steps: Call getShaderPrecisionFormat for VERTEX and FRAGMENT x LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH x FLOAT, INT

limits.headline: Can check how precise your graphics chip maths is, to guess your chip family
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the page loads
can: Check number precision limits in the graphics chip
Tell desktop, Apple, Adreno, Mali and PowerVR families apart
Add that clue to a device profile
cannot: Name your exact device by itself

story.what_it_is: A script reads the number ranges your graphics chip supports for floats and integers.

marketing.name: getShaderPrecisionFormat
marketing.pitch: Reports the range and precision a graphics chip supports for numbers used in shaders.

story.for_you: You never see it. Your browser reports how exactly your graphics chip can handle numbers. Phones and laptops differ, so the answers are a small clue about your device.
story.for_makers: Game and graphics code needs this to avoid visual glitches on weaker chips. Fingerprinting tools add it to a bundle, because it cleanly separates mobile and desktop graphics.

use_cases.example: A browser game uses lower precision on phones to run faster, after checking what the chip supports.
A web photo editor with filters picks the right math so colors do not band on older phones.
A web map draws smooth shading only if the chip supports high precision numbers.
A fraud tool checks that the reported graphics type matches the device model.
A tracker adds the precision numbers to the graphics part of a device ID.
A graphics developer logs these numbers to understand why a shader looks broken on one phone.
A web based AR viewer checks precision before it enables advanced lighting.

technical_bounds: Low entropy alone; useful to pin GPU family
